decks.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers — Part 1: Decimals, proofs and the number line
goals: Classify numbers as natural, whole, integer, rational or irrational
Change terminating and recurring decimals to fractions
Prove by contradiction that root two, root three and root five are irrational
Mark rational numbers and square roots on the number line by construction

slides.heading: Rational and Irrational Numbers, Part 1
slides.body_md: Every real number is rational or irrational. Its decimal expansion tells you which.

nodes.label: It never stops and never repeats

visual.alt: Flow chart: look at the decimal expansion. If it stops or a block repeats, the number is rational and equals p over q. If it neither stops nor repeats, the number is irrational.
visual.caption: Terminating or recurring means rational; neither means irrational.

slides.narration: Welcome to rational and irrational numbers. Every real number is one or the other, and its decimal expansion tells you which. If the decimal stops or repeats a block, the number is rational. If it never stops and never repeats, it is irrational. In this part we also prove that root two is irrational and mark roots on the number line.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: **Classify** numbers: natural, whole, integer, rational, irrational
Mark numbers on the **number line** by construction
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. First we sort numbers into families. Then we convert recurring decimals to fractions. Then we meet proof by contradiction, and finally we use right triangles to mark square roots on the number line.

slides.heading: The families of numbers
slides.body_md: Natural numbers sit inside whole numbers, which sit inside integers, which sit inside **rational numbers**. Irrational numbers are the real numbers outside the rationals.

visual.alt: Table classifying seven numbers. Seven is natural, whole, integer and rational. Zero is whole, integer and rational but not natural. Minus twelve over four equals minus three, an integer and rational. Five eighths and zero point three recurring are rational but not integers. Root twenty is irrational. Root of eighty one over four equals nine over two, which is rational.
visual.caption: Every row is checked: a number is irrational exactly when it is not rational.

slides.narration: Look at the table. Seven is natural, whole, integer and rational. Zero is not natural, but it is whole. Minus twelve over four is minus three, an integer. Five eighths and zero point three recurring are rational but not integers. Only root twenty is irrational. Always simplify first: the root of eighty one over four is nine halves, which is rational.

slides.heading: Fractions and their decimals
slides.body_md: A fraction in lowest terms has a **terminating** decimal only if its denominator has no prime factor except $2$ and $5$. Otherwise the decimal **recurs**.

visual.alt: Table of six fractions and their decimals. Seven sixteenths is zero point four three seven five, terminating; nine twentieths is zero point four five, terminating. Four elevenths, eleven thirtieths, two sevenths and five twelfths recur. Only denominators with the prime factors two and five terminate.
visual.caption: A fraction in lowest terms terminates only when its denominator is $2^a \times 5^b$.

slides.narration: Divide the numerator by the denominator and look at what happens. Seven sixteenths and nine twentieths stop, because their denominators are made only of twos and fives. Four elevenths, eleven thirtieths, two sevenths and five twelfths recur, because they hide a three, seven or eleven in the denominator. Either way, the number is rational.

slides.heading: Quick check: recurring decimals
slides.body_md: Can every recurring decimal be a fraction?
slides.narration: Think about what multiplying by a power of ten and subtracting does to the repeating part.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a recurring decimal
slides.body_md: Write $0.\overline{72}$ as a fraction in lowest terms.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Let $x = 0.\overline{72}$. Two digits repeat, so multiply by $100$: $100x = 72.\overline{72}$.

visual.alt: Table of four steps to convert zero point seven two recurring to a fraction: name it x; multiply by one hundred; subtract to get ninety nine x equals seventy two; then x equals seventy two over ninety nine, which is eight elevenths.
visual.caption: Multiply by $10^k$, where $k$ digits repeat, and subtract.

slides.narration: Call the number x. Two digits repeat, so multiply by one hundred. Now the repeating parts are identical, and subtracting removes them: ninety nine x equals seventy two. So x is seventy two over ninety nine, and dividing top and bottom by nine gives eight elevenths. Check by long division: eight divided by eleven gives zero point seven two recurring.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: some digits do not repeat
slides.body_md: Write $2.5\overline{6}$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

rows: Move the point past the non-repeating digit
Move it past one repeating block as well

visual.alt: Table of five steps to convert two point five six recurring: ten x equals twenty five point six recurring; one hundred x equals two hundred fifty six point six recurring; subtracting gives ninety x equals two hundred thirty one; so x is seventy seven thirtieths.
visual.caption: Two multipliers, $10x$ and $100x$, line up the repeating parts.

slides.narration: Here the five does not repeat, only the six does. Multiply by ten to move the point past the five, and by one hundred to move it past one six as well. Both numbers end in the same repeating tail, so subtracting leaves ninety x equals two hundred thirty one. Reduce by three to get seventy seven thirtieths.

slides.heading: Quick check: the repeating block
slides.body_md: Use long division and keep track of remainders.
slides.narration: Divide three by thirteen, writing each remainder. When a remainder repeats, the digits repeat. Add the digits in the block.

slides.heading: Irrational numbers
slides.body_md: A number is **irrational** if it cannot be written as $\dfrac{p}{q}$ with integers $p$ and $q \ne 0$. Its decimal never stops and never repeats.

rows: no block repeats and it never stops (proved by contradiction)
no block repeats and it never stops (proved by contradiction)
no block repeats and it never stops (proved by contradiction)
the gaps keep growing, so no block repeats

visual.alt: Table of irrational numbers: root two is one point four one four two one three six, root three is one point seven three two zero five zero eight, root five is two point two three six zero six eight, and a pattern decimal whose zeros keep increasing. None repeats and none stops.
visual.caption: An irrational number has a non-terminating, non-recurring decimal.

slides.narration: Some numbers cannot be written as a fraction. Root two, root three and root five are the most famous. Their decimals go on for ever without a repeating block. A pattern decimal such as zero point one zero one zero zero one also never repeats, because the gaps keep growing. Together, rational and irrational numbers make up the real numbers.

slides.heading: Combining rational and irrational numbers
slides.body_md: Rational + irrational is always irrational. But irrational + irrational, or irrational × irrational, can be either.

visual.alt: Table of six examples. Rational plus rational is rational. Rational plus irrational, three plus root two, is irrational. Two irrationals can add to a rational: root two plus three minus root two is three. Rational times irrational is irrational. Two irrationals can multiply to a rational, root two times root eight is four, or to an irrational, root three times root five.
visual.caption: The sum or product of two irrational numbers may be rational or irrational.

slides.narration: What happens when we combine them? A rational plus an irrational is always irrational. But two irrational numbers can add to a rational: root two plus three minus root two is exactly three. And root two times root eight is four. So never assume that the sum or product of irrational numbers is irrational.

slides.heading: Proof by contradiction
slides.body_md: To prove a statement, **assume it is false**, argue correctly, and reach something impossible. Then the assumption must be wrong.

visual.alt: Flow chart of the proof that root two is irrational: assume root two is p over q in lowest terms; square to get p squared equals two q squared; p is even; put p equal to two k, so q squared is two k squared; q is even too; p and q share the factor two, a contradiction; so root two is irrational.
visual.caption: Seven steps: assume, square, parity of $p$, parity of $q$, contradiction, conclude.

slides.narration: Here is the whole proof that root two is irrational. Assume root two is p over q in lowest terms. Squaring gives p squared equals two q squared, so p is even. Write p as two k. Then q squared is two k squared, so q is even as well. But then p and q share the factor two, which contradicts lowest terms. So the assumption was wrong.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: why "even squared" matters
slides.body_md: Why does "$p^2$ is even" force "$p$ is even"?
bullets: The square of an **odd** number is odd.
So if $p$ were odd, $p^2$ would be odd.
But $p^2 = 2q^2$ is even, so $p$ must be even.

visual.alt: Table for n from one to eight: n squared is odd exactly when n is odd, and even exactly when n is even. For example three squared is nine, odd, and four squared is sixteen, even.
visual.caption: $n^2$ has the same parity as $n$, so $p^2$ even forces $p$ even.

slides.narration: The step from p squared even to p even is the key. Look at the table: when n is odd, n squared is odd, and when n is even, n squared is even. So an even square can only come from an even number. In the proof, two q squared is even, so p squared is even, and so p is even.

slides.heading: Quick check: the proof
slides.body_md: Which conclusion follows from $p^2 = 2q^2$?
slides.narration: Decide whether p squared is even or odd, then use what the table showed about squares and parity.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the proof for the square root of three
slides.body_md: What changes for $\sqrt{3}$? We use **divisibility by $3$** instead of "even".
bullets: So $3 \mid p^2$, hence $3 \mid p$ (because $3$ is prime). Write $p = 3k$.
Then $9k^2 = 3q^2$, so $q^2 = 3k^2$ and $3 \mid q$: both divisible by $3$, a contradiction.

visual.alt: Table for p from six to eleven. When p is divisible by three, p squared is divisible by three. When p leaves remainder one or two, p squared leaves remainder one. So three divides p squared only if three divides p.
visual.caption: $3 \mid p^2$ exactly when $3 \mid p$: this drives the proof for $\sqrt{3}$.

slides.narration: For root three the argument is the same, with three in place of two. Assume root three is p over q. Then p squared is three q squared, so three divides p squared. The table shows that three divides a square only when three divides the number itself. So p is three k, q squared is three k squared, and three divides q too. That contradicts lowest terms.

slides.heading: Rational numbers on the number line
slides.body_md: To mark $\dfrac{7}{3}$: it is $2 + \dfrac{1}{3}$. Cut the unit from $2$ to $3$ into **three equal parts** and take the first mark.

visual.alt: Number line from one to three with each unit cut into three equal parts. The point seven thirds is marked: two plus one third, the first mark after two.
visual.caption: $\dfrac{7}{3} = 2 + \dfrac{1}{3}$: cut the unit from $2$ to $3$ into three equal parts and take the first mark.

slides.narration: Rational numbers are marked by equal division. Seven thirds is two and one third. So find two and three, cut the gap into three equal parts, and take the first mark after two. The same method works for any fraction: split the unit into as many equal parts as the denominator.

slides.heading: Marking root two
slides.body_md: Draw $OA = 1$ and $AB = 1$ at right angles. By Pythagoras, $OB = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}$. Swing an arc from $O$ through $B$ to the line.

visual.alt: Number line with zero, one and two marked. At the point one a vertical segment of length one is drawn up to point B. A circle centred at zero passes through B and cuts the number line at the point labelled root two, between one and two.
visual.caption: A unit right triangle: $OB = \sqrt{2}$, and the circle with centre $O$ and radius $OB$ meets the line at $P$.

slides.narration: To mark root two, start at zero and one on the number line. At one, draw a segment of length one at right angles to the line. The hypotenuse from zero to this point has length root of one plus one, which is root two. Put the compass point at zero and swing an arc through the top of the triangle. It meets the line at root two, between one point four and one point five.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: marking root five
slides.body_md: Use legs $2$ and $1$: $OB = \sqrt{2^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{5}$. For $\sqrt{13}$ use legs $3$ and $2$, since $3^2 + 2^2 = 13$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Choose whole numbers $a$ and $b$ with $a^2 + b^2 = 5$: $a = 2$, $b = 1$.
**Step 2 —** Draw $OA = 2$, then $AB = 1$ at right angles to the line.
**Step 3 —** Arc with centre $O$ and radius $OB$ meets the line at $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236$.

visual.alt: Number line with zero, one, two and three marked. At the point two a vertical segment of length one is drawn up to point B. A circle centred at zero passes through B and cuts the number line at the point labelled root five, between two and three.
visual.caption: A right triangle with legs $2$ and $1$: $OB = \sqrt{5}$, and the circle with centre $O$ and radius $OB$ meets the line at $P$.

slides.narration: For root five, write five as a sum of two squares: four plus one. So the legs are two and one. Draw two along the line, one at right angles, and swing the arc from zero. It lands between two and three, at about two point two three six. For root thirteen you would use legs three and two, because nine plus four is thirteen.

slides.heading: Quick check: where is seven quarters?
slides.body_md: Cut a unit into equal parts.
slides.narration: Write seven quarters as a whole number plus a fraction, then decide which interval to cut and how many equal parts to make.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Recurring decimal to fraction: multiply by $10^k$, subtract
Proof by contradiction: assume, deduce, contradict, conclude
Number line: equal division for fractions; right triangles for roots

rows: rationals by division; roots by right triangles

visual.alt: Summary table for part one: rational numbers are p over q with terminating or recurring decimals; irrational numbers have non-terminating, non-recurring decimals; recurring decimals are converted by multiplying by a power of ten and subtracting; proofs by contradiction assume, deduce, contradict and conclude; roots are marked with right triangles.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. Rational numbers are fractions, with decimals that stop or repeat. Irrational numbers never stop and never repeat. To convert a recurring decimal, multiply by a power of ten and subtract. Roots like root two are proved irrational by contradiction, and are marked on the number line with a right triangle and a compass arc.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Recurring decimal (3 marks):** the multiples of $x$ 1 + subtraction 1 + fraction in lowest terms 1
**Proof (long answer):** assumption in lowest terms 1 + $p^2$ step 2 + second variable 2 + contradiction 1
**Mistake:** forgetting "in lowest terms" at the start of the proof
**Mistake:** treating the non-repeating digits as part of the block
**Mistake:** claiming that the sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational
slides.narration: In a proof, always begin with the assumption in lowest terms, and say clearly where the contradiction is. For recurring decimals, show both multiples of x and the subtraction, and reduce the fraction. Do not mix up the digits that repeat with those that do not. And remember that two irrational numbers can add up to a rational one.

decks.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers — Part 2: Surds and rationalising the denominator
goals: Say what a surd is and simplify surds
Add, subtract, multiply and compare surds
Find the rationalising factor of a binomial surd
Rationalise denominators and find a and b in expressions of the form a plus b root c

slides.heading: Surds, Part 2
slides.body_md: A surd is an irrational root, such as $\sqrt{27}$ or $\sqrt{45}$. This part is about simplifying them and clearing them from denominators.

visual.alt: Table of five square roots. Root twenty seven is three root three, a surd. Root forty nine is seven, rational. The root of sixteen over twenty five is four fifths, rational. Root zero point zero nine is zero point three, rational. Root forty five is three root five, a surd.
visual.caption: A surd is an irrational root of a rational number.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two, on surds. A surd is an irrational root of a rational number. Root twenty seven is a surd, but root forty nine is not, because it is just seven. In this part you will simplify surds, combine them, compare them, and remove them from the bottom of a fraction.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **conjugate** of a binomial surd
Find $a$ and $b$ when a result equals $a + b\sqrt{c}$
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We simplify surds, add and subtract the like ones, multiply them and put them in order. Then we meet conjugates, which let us remove surds from denominators, and finally we find the numbers a and b in results of the form a plus b root c.

slides.heading: What is a surd?
slides.body_md: A **surd** is an irrational number that is a root of a rational number. $\sqrt{2}$ is a surd of **order** $2$ (a square root); $\sqrt[3]{5}$ is a surd of order $3$. In this chapter we work with square roots.

visual.alt: Table of five square roots. Root twenty seven is three root three, a surd. Root forty nine is seven, rational. The root of sixteen over twenty five is four fifths, rational. Root zero point zero nine is zero point three, rational. Root forty five is three root five, a surd.
visual.caption: A surd is an irrational root of a rational number.

slides.narration: A surd is an irrational root of a rational number. The order of a surd is the index of the root: a square root has order two, and a cube root has order three. Always simplify before you decide. Root zero point zero nine looks like a surd, but it equals zero point three, so it is rational.

slides.heading: Simplifying a surd
slides.body_md: $\sqrt{a^2 b} = a\sqrt{b}$. Find the **largest square factor** and take its root out.

visual.alt: Table of five simplifications. Root seventy two is root thirty six times two, six root two. Root ninety eight is seven root two. Root one hundred fifty is five root six. Root two hundred forty five is seven root five. Root three hundred ninety six is six root eleven.
visual.caption: Write the number under the root as a perfect square times a number with no square factor.

slides.narration: To simplify a surd, look for a perfect square that divides the number. Root seventy two is root thirty six times two, which is six root two. Root two hundred forty five is seven root five. A surd is simplest when the number under the root has no square factor left.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a square tile
slides.body_md: An imagined square tile has area $1008$ cm$^2$. Find its side in simplest surd form.
bullets: **Step 2 —** The largest square factor of $1008$ is $144$: $1008 = 144 \times 7$.

visual.alt: Table testing perfect squares against one thousand eight. Four, nine, sixteen, thirty six and one hundred forty four all divide it, leaving two hundred fifty two, one hundred twelve, sixty three, twenty eight and seven. The largest, one hundred forty four, leaves seven, which has no square factor.
visual.caption: Use the largest square factor, $144$; the quotient $7$ has no square factor left.

slides.narration: The side of the tile is the square root of one thousand and eight. Try perfect squares. Four, nine, sixteen and thirty six all divide it, but the largest is one hundred forty four, which leaves seven. Seven has no square factor, so the side is twelve root seven centimetres. Using a smaller square factor first would only mean more steps.

slides.heading: Like and unlike surds
slides.body_md: **Like surds** have the same surd after simplifying, so they can be added or subtracted like $3x + 5x$. **Unlike surds** cannot be combined.

visual.alt: Table of three pairs. Root eighteen and root fifty simplify to three root two and five root two, like surds. Root twelve and root twenty seven simplify to two root three and three root three, like surds. Root twenty is two root five and root thirty cannot be simplified, so these are unlike surds.
visual.caption: Only like surds can be added or subtracted.

slides.narration: Surds behave like algebra letters. Three root two plus five root two is eight root two, just as three x plus five x is eight x. But root two plus root three cannot be combined. So simplify each surd first, and only then see whether they are like or unlike.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: adding and subtracting
slides.body_md: Simplify $4\sqrt{20} + 3\sqrt{45} - \sqrt{80}$.

rows: They are like surds: combine the coefficients

visual.alt: Table of three steps: simplify four root twenty to eight root five, three root forty five to nine root five and root eighty to four root five; combine the coefficients; the answer is thirteen root five.
visual.caption: Simplify first, then combine like surds.

slides.narration: First simplify each surd. Four root twenty is eight root five. Three root forty five is nine root five. Root eighty is four root five. Now all three are multiples of root five, so combine the coefficients: eight plus nine minus four is thirteen. The answer is thirteen root five.

slides.heading: Quick check: a craftsman's braid
slides.body_md: Simplify each piece, then combine.
slides.narration: Simplify each of the three surds to a multiple of the same surd, then add the two pieces and take off the trimmed length.

slides.heading: Multiplying and dividing surds
slides.body_md: $\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{b} = \sqrt{ab}$ and $\dfrac{\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{b}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{a}{b}}$. Multiply the numbers outside the roots separately.

visual.alt: Table of four products and quotients of surds: root six times root ten is two root fifteen; two root three times five root six is thirty root two; root seventy two over root eight is three; six root fourteen over three root two is two root seven.
visual.caption: Multiply coefficients with coefficients and surds with surds; then simplify.

slides.narration: To multiply surds, multiply the numbers outside and the numbers inside separately, then simplify. Root six times root ten is root sixty, which is two root fifteen. Two root three times five root six is ten root eighteen, which is thirty root two. Division works the same way, and sometimes gives a rational answer.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a product of binomial surds
slides.body_md: Expand $(3 + 2\sqrt{5})(4 - \sqrt{5})$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** Add the rational parts and the surd parts.

visual.alt: Multiplication grid for three plus two root five times four minus root five. Three times four is twelve; three times minus root five is minus three root five; two root five times four is eight root five; two root five times minus root five is minus ten. Adding, the product is two plus five root five.
visual.caption: Add the four boxes: $12 - 10 = 2$ and $-3\sqrt{5} + 8\sqrt{5} = 5\sqrt{5}$.

slides.narration: Multiply every term in the first bracket by every term in the second. Three times four is twelve. Three times minus root five is minus three root five. Two root five times four is eight root five. And two root five times minus root five is minus ten, because root five times root five is five. Add: twelve minus ten is two, and the surds give five root five.

slides.heading: Comparing surds
slides.body_md: To put surds in order, write each as a single root, or square each, and compare the numbers.

visual.alt: Table comparing three ribbon lengths. Three root seven is root sixty three; two root fifteen is root sixty; four root three is root forty eight. The order from longest is three root seven, two root fifteen, four root three.
visual.caption: Put every surd under one root sign (or square it) and compare the numbers.

slides.narration: To compare surds, bring each one under a single root sign. Three root seven is root sixty three. Two root fifteen is root sixty. Four root three is root forty eight. The larger the number under the root, the longer the ribbon. So the order, longest first, is three root seven, then two root fifteen, then four root three.

slides.heading: Quick check: which is a surd?
slides.body_md: Simplify before you decide.
slides.narration: Simplify each square root. Only the one that is irrational, and not a rational number in disguise, is a surd.

slides.heading: Conjugates and rationalising factors
slides.body_md: The **conjugate** of $a + b\sqrt{c}$ is $a - b\sqrt{c}$. Their product $a^2 - b^2c$ is **rational**, so each is a **rationalising factor** of the other.

visual.alt: Table of three binomial surds with their conjugates and products: three plus root five times three minus root five is four; two root three plus one times two root three minus one is eleven; root seven minus root two times root seven plus root two is five. Every product is rational.
visual.caption: The product of conjugates is $a^2 - b^2c$, a rational number.

slides.narration: A binomial surd has two terms, one of them a surd. Its conjugate has the opposite sign in the middle. Multiply them and the middle terms cancel, leaving a squared minus b squared c, which is rational. So the conjugate is a rationalising factor. For a single term such as root five, the rationalising factor is root five itself.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: rationalising a denominator
slides.body_md: Rationalise the denominator of $\dfrac{8}{5 - \sqrt{17}}$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate $5 + \sqrt{17}$.

rows: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate

visual.alt: Table of three steps for eight over five minus root seventeen: multiply by the conjugate five plus root seventeen; the denominator is twenty five minus seventeen, eight; cancel to get five plus root seventeen.
visual.caption: The denominator becomes rational: $25 - 17 = 8$.

slides.narration: The denominator is five minus root seventeen. Multiply top and bottom by its conjugate, five plus root seventeen. At the bottom, the product of conjugates is twenty five minus seventeen, which is eight. The eight on top cancels the eight below, leaving five plus root seventeen, with no surd in the denominator.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: surds in both terms
slides.body_md: Rationalise $\dfrac{2\sqrt{3} + 1}{3\sqrt{3} - 2}$.

visual.alt: Table for two root three plus one over three root three minus two: the conjugate is three root three plus two; the denominator is twenty seven minus four, twenty three; the numerator is twenty plus seven root three; the answer is twenty plus seven root three over twenty three.
visual.caption: Square the root term before subtracting: $(3\sqrt{3})^2 = 27$, not $9$.

slides.narration: Multiply top and bottom by three root three plus two. At the bottom, square three root three to get twenty seven, subtract four, and you have twenty three. At the top, expand: eighteen plus four root three plus three root three plus two, which is twenty plus seven root three. Be careful to square the whole term three root three, not just the root.

slides.heading: Quick check: a rationalising factor
slides.body_md: Which factor makes the product rational?
slides.narration: Multiply the binomial by each option and look for the one whose product has no surd left.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: finding a and b
slides.body_md: Find rational $a$ and $b$ if $\dfrac{\sqrt{7} + 2}{\sqrt{7} - 2} = a + b\sqrt{7}$.

rows: Multiply by $\sqrt{7} + 2$ on top and bottom

visual.alt: Table of four steps for root seven plus two over root seven minus two: multiply by root seven plus two; the numerator is eleven plus four root seven and the denominator is three; so a is eleven thirds and b is four thirds.
visual.caption: Split the fraction into a rational part and a surd part to read $a$ and $b$.

slides.narration: To find a and b, first rationalise the fraction. Multiply by root seven plus two on top and bottom. The denominator is seven minus four, which is three. The numerator is the square of root seven plus two: eleven plus four root seven. Split the fraction into a rational part, eleven thirds, and a surd part, four thirds of root seven.

slides.heading: A useful shortcut: conjugate fractions
slides.body_md: $\dfrac{1}{a + b\sqrt{c}} + \dfrac{1}{a - b\sqrt{c}} = \dfrac{2a}{a^2 - b^2c}$. The surds cancel when you add.

rows: Add: common denominator is the product of conjugates

visual.alt: Table of four steps adding one over five plus two root three and one over five minus two root three: the common denominator is twenty five minus twelve, thirteen; the numerator is ten; the sum is ten thirteenths.
visual.caption: In general $\dfrac{1}{a + b\sqrt{c}} + \dfrac{1}{a - b\sqrt{c}} = \dfrac{2a}{a^2 - b^2c}$.

slides.narration: When two conjugate fractions are added, the common denominator is the product of the conjugates, which is rational. In the numerator the surds cancel, leaving two a. For one over five plus two root three plus one over five minus two root three, we get ten over twenty five minus twelve, which is ten thirteenths.

slides.heading: Quick check: find b
slides.body_md: Rationalise, then read the coefficient.
slides.narration: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator. Notice that the new denominator is one, and read off the coefficient of root two.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $\sqrt{a^2 b} = a\sqrt{b}$: take out the largest square
Compare by writing under one root
Rationalise with the conjugate: $(a + b\sqrt{c})(a - b\sqrt{c}) = a^2 - b^2c$

rows: put under one root or square

visual.alt: Summary table for part two: simplify with root of a squared b equals a root b; add like surds only; multiply with root a times root b equals root of ab; compare by squaring; rationalise with the conjugate, whose product is a squared minus b squared c.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. Simplify surds by taking out the largest square. Add and subtract like surds only. Multiply surds under one root, and compare them by squaring. notes.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. The number families and decimals
sections.body_md:
Natural numbers $\subset$ whole numbers $\subset$ integers $\subset$ rational numbers. A **rational number** is $\dfrac{p}{q}$ with integers $p$, $q$ and $q \ne 0$; every integer is rational ($n = \dfrac{n}{1}$).

- A fraction in lowest terms has a **terminating** decimal exactly when its denominator is $2^a \times 5^b$; otherwise the decimal **recurs**.
- Simplify before classifying: $\sqrt{\dfrac{81}{4}} = \dfrac{9}{2}$ is rational.
- A number that is not rational is **irrational**; together they make up the **real numbers**.

key_terms.definition_md: A number that can be written as $\dfrac{p}{q}$ with integers $p$, $q$ and $q \ne 0$; its decimal terminates or recurs.
A real number that is not rational; its decimal never terminates and never recurs.
All rational and irrational numbers together.

visual.alt: Table classifying seven numbers. Seven is natural, whole, integer and rational. Zero is whole, integer and rational but not natural. Minus twelve over four equals minus three, an integer and rational. Five eighths and zero point three recurring are rational but not integers. Root twenty is irrational. Root of eighty one over four equals nine over two, which is rational.

Four elevenths, eleven thirtieths, two sevenths and five twelfths recur. Only denominators with the prime factors two and five terminate.

sections.heading: 2. Recurring decimals as fractions
sections.body_md:
Let $x$ be the decimal. If $k$ digits repeat straight after the point, multiply by $10^k$ and subtract: $100x - x = 72$ gives $0.\overline{72} = \dfrac{72}{99} = \dfrac{8}{11}$.

If some digits do not repeat, use two multipliers so that the repeating tails line up: for $2.5\overline{6}$, $100x - 10x = 231$, so $x = \dfrac{231}{90} = \dfrac{77}{30}$.

Always reduce the fraction, and check with long division.

key_terms.definition_md: A decimal in which a block of digits repeats for ever, written with a bar, as in $0.\overline{72}$.

visual.alt: Table of four steps to convert zero point seven two recurring to a fraction: name it x; multiply by one hundred; subtract to get ninety nine x equals seventy two; then x equals seventy two over ninety nine, which is eight elevenths.
visual.caption: Multiply by $10^k$, where $k$ digits repeat, and subtract.

rows: Move the point past the non-repeating digit
Move it past one repeating block as well

sections.heading: 3. Irrational numbers and the real numbers
sections.body_md:
$\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{5}$ are irrational, and so is any decimal that neither stops nor repeats, such as $0.1010010001\ldots$.

- rational $+$ irrational and rational $\times$ non-zero irrational are **irrational**.
- two irrational numbers can combine to a rational number: $\sqrt{2} + (3 - \sqrt{2}) = 3$ and $\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{8} = 4$.
- Between any two real numbers there are infinitely many rational and infinitely many irrational numbers.

key_terms.definition_md: A decimal that never stops and never repeats a block: the mark of an irrational number.

rows: no block repeats and it never stops (proved by contradiction)
no block repeats and it never stops (proved by contradiction)
no block repeats and it never stops (proved by contradiction)
the gaps keep growing, so no block repeats

visual.alt: Table of irrational numbers: root two is one point four one four two one three six, root three is one point seven three two zero five zero eight, root five is two point two three six zero six eight, and a pattern decimal whose zeros keep increasing. None repeats and none stops.
visual.caption: An irrational number has a non-terminating, non-recurring decimal.

visuals.alt: Table of six examples. Rational plus rational is rational. Rational plus irrational, three plus root two, is irrational. Two irrationals can add to a rational: root two plus three minus root two is three. Rational times irrational is irrational. Two irrationals can multiply to a rational, root two times root eight is four, or to an irrational, root three times root five.
visuals.caption: The sum or product of two irrational numbers may be rational or irrational.

nodes.label: It never stops and never repeats

visuals.alt: Flow chart: look at the decimal expansion. If it stops or a block repeats, the number is rational and equals p over q. If it neither stops nor repeats, the number is irrational.
visuals.caption: Terminating or recurring means rational; neither means irrational.

sections.heading: 4. Proofs of irrationality
sections.body_md:
**Proof by contradiction:** assume the opposite, argue, and reach something impossible.

For $\sqrt{2}$: assume $\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{p}{q}$ in lowest terms. Then $p^2 = 2q^2$, so $p^2$ is even, so $p$ is even; write $p = 2k$, then $q^2 = 2k^2$ and $q$ is even. So $p$ and $q$ share the factor $2$: a contradiction.

For $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{5}$ use the prime $3$ or $5$: if a prime divides $p^2$, it divides $p$. The method fails for a perfect square such as $\sqrt{9}$, which is rational.

To show $a + b\sqrt{c}$ irrational ($b \ne 0$), assume it equals a rational $r$ and isolate the surd.

key_terms.definition_md: Assume the statement is false and show that this leads to something impossible.
$\dfrac{p}{q}$ where $p$ and $q$ have no common factor except $1$.

visual.alt: Flow chart of the proof that root two is irrational: assume root two is p over q in lowest terms; square to get p squared equals two q squared; p is even; put p equal to two k, so q squared is two k squared; q is even too; p and q share the factor two, a contradiction; so root two is irrational.
visual.caption: Seven steps: assume, square, parity of $p$, parity of $q$, contradiction, conclude.

visuals.alt: Table for n from one to eight: n squared is odd exactly when n is odd, and even exactly when n is even. For example three squared is nine, odd, and four squared is sixteen, even.
visuals.caption: $n^2$ has the same parity as $n$, so $p^2$ even forces $p$ even.

visuals.alt: Table for p from six to eleven. When p is divisible by three, p squared is divisible by three. When p leaves remainder one or two, p squared leaves remainder one. So three divides p squared only if three divides p.
visuals.caption: $3 \mid p^2$ exactly when $3 \mid p$: this drives the proof for $\sqrt{3}$.

sections.heading: 5. The number line
sections.body_md:
**Rationals:** write the number as a whole number plus a fraction, cut the unit into as many equal parts as the denominator, and count: $\dfrac{7}{3} = 2 + \dfrac{1}{3}$.

**Square roots:** to mark $\sqrt{n}$, write $n = a^2 + b^2$ with whole numbers $a$, $b$; draw $OA = a$ along the line and $AB = b$ at right angles; $OB = \sqrt{n}$ by Pythagoras. With centre $O$ and radius $OB$, swing an arc to the line.

$\sqrt{2}$: legs $1, 1$. $\sqrt{5}$: legs $2, 1$. $\sqrt{13}$: legs $3, 2$. A negative root, $-\sqrt{5}$, is cut on the left of $O$ with the same radius.

key_terms.definition_md: A right triangle whose hypotenuse is $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, copied on to the number line with a compass arc.

visual.alt: Number line from one to three with each unit cut into three equal parts. The point seven thirds is marked: two plus one third, the first mark after two.
visual.caption: $\dfrac{7}{3} = 2 + \dfrac{1}{3}$: cut the unit from $2$ to $3$ into three equal parts and take the first mark.

visuals.alt: Number line with zero, one and two marked. At the point one a vertical segment of length one is drawn up to point B. A circle centred at zero passes through B and cuts the number line at the point labelled root two, between one and two.
visuals.caption: A unit right triangle: $OB = \sqrt{2}$, and the circle with centre $O$ and radius $OB$ meets the line at $P$.

visuals.alt: Number line with zero, one, two and three marked. At the point two a vertical segment of length one is drawn up to point B. A circle centred at zero passes through B and cuts the number line at the point labelled root five, between two and three.
visuals.caption: A right triangle with legs $2$ and $1$: $OB = \sqrt{5}$, and the circle with centre $O$ and radius $OB$ meets the line at $P$.

sections.heading: 6. Surds: simplifying and combining
sections.body_md:
A **surd** is an irrational root of a rational number, for example $\sqrt{27}$; $\sqrt{2}$ has **order** $2$ and $\sqrt[3]{5}$ order $3$. Here we use square roots.

- Simplify: $\sqrt{a^2 b} = a\sqrt{b}$ (largest square factor): $\sqrt{1008} = 12\sqrt{7}$.
- Add or subtract **like surds** only: $4\sqrt{20} + 3\sqrt{45} - \sqrt{80} = 13\sqrt{5}$.
- Multiply: $\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{b} = \sqrt{ab}$; expand brackets term by term.
- Compare by writing each as a single root (or squaring): $3\sqrt{7} > 2\sqrt{15} > 4\sqrt{3}$.

key_terms.definition_md: An irrational root of a rational number, such as $\sqrt{27}$.
Surds that have the same surd part after simplifying, such as $3\sqrt{2}$ and $5\sqrt{2}$.
The index of the root: $2$ for a square root.

visual.alt: Table of five simplifications. Root seventy two is root thirty six times two, six root two. Root ninety eight is seven root two. Root one hundred fifty is five root six. Root two hundred forty five is seven root five. Root three hundred ninety six is six root eleven.
visual.caption: Write the number under the root as a perfect square times a number with no square factor.

visuals.alt: Table of three pairs. Root eighteen and root fifty simplify to three root two and five root two, like surds. Root twelve and root twenty seven simplify to two root three and three root three, like surds. Root twenty is two root five and root thirty cannot be simplified, so these are unlike surds.
visuals.caption: Only like surds can be added or subtracted.

visuals.alt: Table of four products and quotients of surds: root six times root ten is two root fifteen; two root three times five root six is thirty root two; root seventy two over root eight is three; six root fourteen over three root two is two root seven.
visuals.caption: Multiply coefficients with coefficients and surds with surds; then simplify.

visuals.alt: Table comparing three ribbon lengths. Three root seven is root sixty three; two root fifteen is root sixty; four root three is root forty eight. The order from longest is three root seven, two root fifteen, four root three.
visuals.caption: Put every surd under one root sign (or square it) and compare the numbers.

sections.heading: 7. Rationalising the denominator
sections.body_md:
A single surd $\sqrt{c}$ is rationalised by multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt{c}$: $\dfrac{12}{5\sqrt{6}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}$.

For a binomial denominator multiply by its **conjugate**: $(a + b\sqrt{c})(a - b\sqrt{c}) = a^2 - b^2c$.

- $\dfrac{8}{5 - \sqrt{17}} = \dfrac{8(5 + \sqrt{17})}{25 - 17} = 5 + \sqrt{17}$.
- To find $a$ and $b$ in $a + b\sqrt{c}$, rationalise and compare the rational and surd parts: $\dfrac{\sqrt{7} + 2}{\sqrt{7} - 2} = \dfrac{11}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{7}$.
- $\dfrac{1}{a + b\sqrt{c}} + \dfrac{1}{a - b\sqrt{c}} = \dfrac{2a}{a^2 - b^2c}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A number that, multiplied by a surd expression, gives a rational number.
The binomial surd $a - b\sqrt{c}$ for $a + b\sqrt{c}$.

visual.alt: Table of three binomial surds with their conjugates and products: three plus root five times three minus root five is four; two root three plus one times two root three minus one is eleven; root seven minus root two times root seven plus root two is five. Every product is rational.
visual.caption: The product of conjugates is $a^2 - b^2c$, a rational number.

visuals.alt: Table of three steps for eight over five minus root seventeen: multiply by the conjugate five plus root seventeen; the denominator is twenty five minus seventeen, eight; cancel to get five plus root seventeen.
visuals.caption: The denominator becomes rational: $25 - 17 = 8$.

visuals.alt: Table for two root three plus one over three root three minus two: the conjugate is three root three plus two; the denominator is twenty seven minus four, twenty three; the numerator is twenty plus seven root three; the answer is twenty plus seven root three over twenty three.
visuals.caption: Square the root term before subtracting: $(3\sqrt{3})^2 = 27$, not $9$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Recurring decimal as a fraction (2–3 marks):* the two multiples of $x$ 1; subtraction 1; fraction in lowest terms 1.
- *Proof of irrationality (long answer):* assumption in lowest terms 1; $p^2$ step 2; second variable 2; contradiction and conclusion 1.
- *Simplify or compare surds (2 marks):* surds simplified 1; result 1.
- *Rationalise (3 marks):* conjugate 1; denominator $a^2 - b^2c$ 1; numerator and simplest form 1.
- *Find $a$ and $b$ (3 marks):* rationalise 1; simplify 1; read off $a$ and $b$ 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c) usually 3 + 3 + 4; show all working.

**Common mistakes**
1. Forgetting "in lowest terms" at the start of a proof of irrationality.
2. Treating non-repeating digits as part of the repeating block.
3. Adding the numbers under two roots: $\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{5} \ne \sqrt{8}$.
4. Squaring only the root in $(3\sqrt{3})^2$.
5. Using $a + b\sqrt{c}$ again, instead of the conjugate $a - b\sqrt{c}$, as the multiplier.
6. Claiming that the sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational, or that every non-terminating decimal is irrational.

questions.stem_md: Meena says that every integer $n$ is a rational number. Which form of $n$ shows why?
questions.solution_md: A rational number is a quotient of two integers with a non-zero denominator. Writing $n = \dfrac{n}{1}$ does exactly that, for $n = -7$, $0$ or $12$ alike. The reciprocal $\dfrac{1}{n}$ fails at $n = 0$.

questions.stem_md: A tailor writes the number $-\dfrac{12}{4}$ on a measuring slip. Which is the smallest of these sets that contains it?

options.text_md: rational numbers that are not integers

questions.solution_md: $-\dfrac{12}{4} = -3$. It is negative, so it is neither natural nor whole; it is an integer, and every integer is rational.

questions.stem_md: A tile shop sells edging strips whose lengths are fractions of a metre. Exactly one of these lengths, in metres, is a terminating decimal. Which one?
questions.solution_md: In lowest terms, a fraction terminates only if its denominator has no prime factor other than $2$ and $5$. $80 = 2^4 \times 5$ qualifies, and $\dfrac{13}{80} = 0.1625$. But $14$ has the factor $7$, and $60$ and $15$ have the factor $3$.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following decimals is an irrational number?

options.text_md: $0.434334333433334\ldots \text{ (each block of 3s is one longer than the last, split by single 4s)}$

questions.solution_md: $0.\overline{45}$ and $3.1\overline{27}$ repeat a block, and $0.5625$ stops, so each is rational. In $0.434334333\ldots$ the run of $3$s grows for ever, so no block repeats and it never stops: it is irrational.

questions.stem_md: Rani combines the surds $\sqrt{12}$, $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{5}$ in four different ways. Which result is a rational number?
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt{12} + \sqrt{3} = 3\sqrt{3}$ is irrational. Squaring it gives $9 \times 3 = 27$, which is rational. $\sqrt{12} \times \sqrt{5} = 2\sqrt{15}$ and $\dfrac{\sqrt{12}}{\sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{15}}{5}$ are irrational.

questions.stem_md: A label on a fabric roll gives the width as $0.272727\ldots$ metres, that is $0.\overline{27}$ m. In lowest terms, this width is
questions.solution_md: Let $x = 0.\overline{27}$. Then $100x = 27.\overline{27}$, so $99x = 27$ and $x = \dfrac{27}{99} = \dfrac{3}{11}$. The fraction $\dfrac{27}{100}$ would be $0.27$, which stops.

questions.stem_md: A tank gauge shows $0.1666\ldots$, that is $0.1\overline{6}$, of full capacity. As a fraction in lowest terms this is
questions.solution_md: Let $x = 0.1\overline{6}$. Then $10x = 1.\overline{6}$ and $100x = 16.\overline{6}$. Subtracting, $90x = 15$, so $x = \dfrac{15}{90} = \dfrac{1}{6}$. The fraction $\dfrac{16}{99}$ treats the $1$ as repeating too.

questions.stem_md: To prove by contradiction that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, we begin by assuming that

options.text_md: $\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{p}{q}, \text{ where } p, q \text{ are integers with no common factor except } 1, q \ne 0$

questions.solution_md: A proof by contradiction assumes the opposite of what we want: $\sqrt{2}$ is rational, so it can be written in lowest terms as $\dfrac{p}{q}$. We then show that this leads to a contradiction.

questions.stem_md: In the proof that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational we reach $p^2 = 2q^2$, where $p$ and $q$ are integers. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.solution_md: The right side $2q^2$ is a multiple of $2$, so $p^2$ is even. The square of an odd number is odd, so $p$ cannot be odd: $p$ is even.

questions.stem_md: Isha copies the proof for $\sqrt{2}$ word for word to "show" that $\sqrt{4}$ is irrational. Which is the first line of her argument that is not valid?

options.text_md: Squaring, $p^2 = 4q^2$, so $p^2$ is even and $p$ is even.
Write $p = 2k$. Then $4k^2 = 4q^2$, so $q$ is even too, which contradicts the assumption.
Suppose $\sqrt{4} = \dfrac{p}{q}$ with $p$ and $q$ having no common factor.

questions.solution_md: With $p = 2k$ we get $4k^2 = 4q^2$, that is $q = k$, which need not be even. Indeed $p = 2$, $q = 1$ has no common factor and gives $\sqrt{4} = 2$. The "q is even too" line is the first to fail.

questions.stem_md: Kavya marks $O$ at $0$ and $A$ at $4$ on a number line. At $A$ she draws a segment $AB$ of length $3$ at right angles to the line, then places a compass point at $O$ with radius $OB$ and cuts the line at $P$. Which number does $P$ represent?
questions.solution_md: By Pythagoras, $OB^2 = 4^2 + 3^2 = 25$, so $OB = 5$. The compass copies this length on to the line, so $P$ is at $5$. It is a rational number, because $25$ is a perfect square.

questions.stem_md: To mark $\sqrt{10}$ on the number line by the right-triangle construction, with $OA$ along the line and $AB$ at right angles, which pair of whole-number lengths should be used?
questions.solution_md: We need $OA^2 + AB^2 = 10$. The pair $3$ and $1$ gives $9 + 1 = 10$. The other pairs give $8$, $5$ and $13$.

questions.stem_md: Which description correctly locates $\dfrac{7}{4}$ on the number line?

options.text_md: Divide the interval from $1$ to $2$ into four equal parts and take the third mark from $1$.
Divide the interval from $1$ to $2$ into seven equal parts and take the fourth mark from $1$.
Divide the interval from $0$ to $1$ into four equal parts and take the third mark from $0$.
Divide the interval from $2$ to $3$ into four equal parts and take the first mark from $2$.

questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{7}{4} = 1 + \dfrac{3}{4}$, so it is three quarters of the way from $1$ to $2$. The other descriptions give $1\dfrac{4}{7}$, $\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $2\dfrac{1}{4}$.

questions.stem_md: A carpenter lists four lengths in metres. Exactly one of them is a surd. Which one?
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt{196} = 14$, $\sqrt{\dfrac{49}{81}} = \dfrac{7}{9}$ and $\sqrt{0.0016} = 0.04$ are all rational. But $135 = 9 \times 15$ is not a perfect square, so $\sqrt{135} = 3\sqrt{15}$ is irrational: a surd.

questions.stem_md: A square floor tile has an area of $432$ cm$^2$. Its side, in centimetres and in simplest surd form, is
questions.solution_md: The side is $\sqrt{432}$. Since $432 = 144 \times 3$, $\sqrt{432} = \sqrt{144} \times \sqrt{3} = 12\sqrt{3}$ cm.

questions.stem_md: Four ribbons have lengths $3\sqrt{5}$ m, $2\sqrt{11}$ m, $4\sqrt{3}$ m and $5\sqrt{2}$ m. Which ribbon is the longest?
questions.solution_md: Compare the squares: $(3\sqrt{5})^2 = 45$, $(2\sqrt{11})^2 = 44$, $(4\sqrt{3})^2 = 48$ and $(5\sqrt{2})^2 = 50$. The largest square belongs to $5\sqrt{2}$.

questions.stem_md: A craftsman joins pieces of braid of lengths $3\sqrt{48}$ cm and $\sqrt{75}$ cm and then trims off $2\sqrt{27}$ cm. The length that remains, in simplest form, is
questions.solution_md: $3\sqrt{48} = 12\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}$ and $2\sqrt{27} = 6\sqrt{3}$. The pieces are like surds, so $12\sqrt{3} + 5\sqrt{3} - 6\sqrt{3} = 11\sqrt{3}$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A rectangular banner is $3\sqrt{6}$ m long and $2\sqrt{10}$ m wide. Its area in square metres, in simplest form, is
questions.solution_md: Area $= 3\sqrt{6} \times 2\sqrt{10} = 6\sqrt{60}$. Since $60 = 4 \times 15$, $\sqrt{60} = 2\sqrt{15}$, so the area is $12\sqrt{15}$.

questions.stem_md: A rationalising factor of the binomial surd $5 - 2\sqrt{3}$ is
questions.solution_md: The conjugate $5 + 2\sqrt{3}$ works: $(5 - 2\sqrt{3})(5 + 2\sqrt{3}) = 25 - 12 = 13$, which is rational. Each of the other three leaves a surd in the product.

questions.stem_md: After the denominator is rationalised, $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{7} - \sqrt{3}}$ becomes
questions.solution_md: Multiply the top and bottom by $\sqrt{7} + \sqrt{3}$. The denominator becomes $7 - 3 = 4$, so the fraction is $\dfrac{6(\sqrt{7} + \sqrt{3})}{4} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{7} + 3\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

questions.stem_md: Two gauges on a machine show the readings $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5} - 2}$ and $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5} + 2}$. The difference between the first reading and the second is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5} - 2} = \sqrt{5} + 2$ and $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5} + 2} = \sqrt{5} - 2$, because $(\sqrt{5} - 2)(\sqrt{5} + 2) = 1$. The difference is $(\sqrt{5} + 2) - (\sqrt{5} - 2) = 4$.

questions.stem_md: If $x = 2 + \sqrt{5}$, then the value of $x^2 - 4x$ is
questions.solution_md: $x^2 = 9 + 4\sqrt{5}$ and $4x = 8 + 4\sqrt{5}$, so $x^2 - 4x = 1$. (Equivalently, $x - 2 = \sqrt{5}$, so $x^2 - 4x + 4 = 5$.)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The decimal $0.4\overline{5}$ is a rational number.

**Reason (R):** Every non-terminating decimal is an irrational number.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $\sqrt{18} + \sqrt{8} = \sqrt{26}$.

**Reason (R):** Square roots of positive numbers obey the product rule $\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{b} = \sqrt{ab}$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $\sqrt{18} + \sqrt{8} = 3\sqrt{2} + 2\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{50}$, not $\sqrt{26}$: A is false. R is the true product rule. Roots of a sum are not the sum of roots. Option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The product $(4 + \sqrt{7})(4 - \sqrt{7})$ is a rational number.

**Reason (R):** For any numbers $a$ and $b$, $(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: By R, the product is $4^2 - (\sqrt{7})^2 = 16 - 7 = 9$, which is rational, so A is true. R is a true identity, and it is exactly why the surd disappears. Option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The number $\sqrt{5}$ can be marked on the number line using a right triangle whose perpendicular sides are $2$ and $1$.

**Reason (R):** The number $\sqrt{5}$ is irrational.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: The hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides $2$ and $1$ has length $\sqrt{4 + 1} = \sqrt{5}$, so A is true. R is also true, but irrationality is not why the construction works; the Pythagoras relation $2^2 + 1^2 = 5$ is. Option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the proof that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational, the step "$3$ divides $p^2$, so $3$ divides $p$" is valid.

**Reason (R):** If a prime divides the product of two integers, it divides at least one of them.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Since $p^2 = p \times p$ and $3$ is prime, $3$ must divide one of the two factors $p$, that is, $3$ divides $p$. So A is true, and R is the rule that justifies it. Option (c).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Assume that $\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{p}{q}$, where $p$ and $q$ are integers with no common factor except $1$ and $q \ne 0$. Show that $p$ is even. [3]

(b) Hence show that $q$ is even too, and state the contradiction. [3]

(c) Using the fact that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, prove that $7 - 4\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Squaring $\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{p}{q}$ gives $2 = \dfrac{p^2}{q^2}$, so $p^2 = 2q^2$. Hence $p^2$ is even, and because the square of an odd number is odd, $p$ is even.

(b) Write $p = 2k$. Then $4k^2 = 2q^2$, so $q^2 = 2k^2$ is even and $q$ is even. Now $p$ and $q$ are both divisible by $2$, which contradicts the assumption that they have no common factor. So $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

(c) Suppose $7 - 4\sqrt{2} = r$, where $r$ is rational. Then $4\sqrt{2} = 7 - r$, so $\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{7 - r}{4}$. The right side is rational, which contradicts the irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$. Hence $7 - 4\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

questions.solution_md: Contradiction proof: parity of $p^2$ and $q^2$, then closure of the rationals.

marking_scheme.step: (a) p squared even, so p even
(b) p = 2k gives q squared = 2 k squared, so q even
(c) Assume 7 - 4 root 2 = r, rational, and isolate root 2

questions.stem_md:
(a) Assume $\sqrt{5} = \dfrac{p}{q}$ in lowest terms and show that $5$ divides $p$. [3]

(b) Hence show that $5$ divides $q$ too, and state the contradiction. [3]

(c) Isha tries the same method on $\sqrt{9}$. Show where it breaks down and say what $\sqrt{9}$ really is. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Squaring gives $p^2 = 5q^2$, so $5$ divides $p^2$. Because $5$ is prime and $p^2 = p \times p$, $5$ divides $p$.

(b) Write $p = 5k$. Then $25k^2 = 5q^2$, so $q^2 = 5k^2$ and $5$ divides $q^2$, hence $5$ divides $q$. So $5$ is a common factor of $p$ and $q$, which contradicts "lowest terms". Therefore $\sqrt{5}$ is irrational.

(c) For $\sqrt{9} = \dfrac{p}{q}$ we get $p^2 = 9q^2$, so $3$ divides $p$; write $p = 3k$. Then $9k^2 = 9q^2$, so $q = k$, and nothing forces $q$ to be divisible by $3$: there is no common factor and no contradiction. Indeed $p = 3$, $q = 1$ works, because $\sqrt{9} = 3$ is rational.

questions.solution_md: Prime divisibility drives the proof; for a perfect square the last step does not give a common factor.

marking_scheme.step: (b) p = 5k gives q squared = 5 k squared, so 5 divides q
(c) p = 3k gives q = k: no common factor forced
